cards.title: Fragile US-Iran Ceasefire Keeps Strait of Hormuz as a Global Oil Shock Trigger
cards.region: Strait of Hormuz / US / Iran / Global
cards.background: Oil prices rose on Friday after the US and Iran exchanged fire in the Strait of Hormuz, the key waterway through which more than a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually passes. Brent crude briefly rose almost 3% to nearly $103 a barrel before easing back to around $100, up from about $70 before the conflict began. The US said it carried out self-defence strikes after 'unprovoked' Iranian attacks on US ships leaving the Gulf, while Iran said the US had violated a ceasefire and attacked its vessels and coastline. President Donald Trump said the ceasefire was still in place and that negotiations with Iran were ongoing.

prop_args.thesis: The exchange shows that even limited military friction in the Strait of Hormuz creates immediate global energy price shocks, so de-escalation and diplomatic management are economically necessary.
mechanisms: First, the Strait of Hormuz is a single-point chokepoint for global energy flows. This is because (1) more than one-fifth of the world's oil and gas usually passes through it, (2) traders price in even small risks of disruption immediately, and (3) any threat to tanker movement forces markets to add a war-risk premium within hours.

Second, the conflict transmits directly into inflation and growth pressures across importing economies. Three reasons: one, Brent jumped almost 3% to nearly $103 a barrel before settling around $100; two, oil was already around $70 before the conflict, so the shock is a large upward reset rather than a marginal move; three, higher fuel costs feed transport, food, and industrial input prices, squeezing households and firms.

Third, a fragile ceasefire is economically preferable to continued brinkmanship because it preserves market confidence. This matters because traders are already treating the truce as unstable, meaning every new exchange of fire compounds uncertainty, discourages investment, and raises hedging costs for shipping and energy firms.

opp_args.thesis: The market reaction is a temporary risk premium, not a structural oil crisis, so the world can absorb the shock if the ceasefire holds and production routes remain open.
mechanisms: First, prices can spike without long-term supply collapse. One, Brent rose to nearly $103 but then fell back to around $100, showing traders still expect flows to continue; two, the US and Iran both publicly downplayed escalation, which signals that neither side wants a full closure of the strait; three, if the waterway remains open, the shock is mostly speculative rather than physical.

Second, the US still has tools to contain escalation and reassure markets. One, Trump said the ceasefire remains in place and negotiations are ongoing; two, US Central Command said it was not seeking to escalate the conflict; three, visible signaling from both sides can stabilize expectations and prevent panic buying.

Third, oil markets are resilient enough to price in geopolitical risk without causing systemic collapse. One, the world has strategic reserves and diversified supply chains; two, traders routinely absorb Middle East tensions as a premium rather than a permanent shortage; three, if the conflict stays limited to isolated exchanges, the macro impact is manageable compared to a true supply cutoff.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the Strait of Hormuz is treated as a temporary headline risk or a durable supply chokepoint. Prop wins if they prove that even brief military exchanges create repeated price shocks and inflationary spillovers; Opp wins if they show the ceasefire is credible enough that markets are only pricing a short-lived premium, not a sustained shortage.
motion_areas: TH, as an oil-importing country, would prioritize de-escalation with Iran over punitive containment
THBT global markets are too dependent on the Strait of Hormuz
THP a world where major energy chokepoints are protected by multilateral guarantees
data_points: Brent crude rose almost 3% to nearly $103 a barrel before falling back to around $100
Oil was trading at around $70 a barrel before the conflict began
More than a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually passes through the Strait of Hormuz
The US said three destroyers were involved in the latest exchange of fire

cards.title: Fragile US-Iran Ceasefire Collapses Into Strait of Hormuz Brinkmanship
cards.region: US / Iran / Strait of Hormuz / UAE
cards.background: On 8 May 2026, the BBC reported that the US and Iran exchanged fire in the Strait of Hormuz even as Donald Trump insisted a ceasefire was still in place. The US said Iranian forces launched missiles, drones and small boats at three US warships, while Iran said the US struck an Iranian oil tanker and coastal areas near Bandar Khamir, Sirik and Qeshm Island. The UAE’s Ministry of Defence also said its air defences were actively engaging an Iranian missile and drone attack, underscoring the regional spillover risk. The flare-up came as Tehran was reportedly considering a US proposal for a 14-point memorandum of understanding and as both sides publicly threatened further escalation if their conditions were not met.

prop_args.thesis: The US should use overwhelming coercive pressure in the Strait of Hormuz to force Iran into a deal before the conflict widens.
mechanisms: First, hard pressure creates bargaining leverage because (1) Iran’s economy and military posture are highly exposed to maritime chokepoints, (2) the regime needs sanctions relief and de-escalation more than the US needs a quick settlement, and (3) visible punishment raises the cost of continued delay, making compromise more attractive than brinkmanship.

Second, limited but forceful retaliation can restore deterrence. Three reasons: one, it signals that attacks on US ships will be met immediately; two, it reduces the incentive for Iran to use deniable proxies and small-boat harassment; three, it reassures Gulf partners like the UAE that the US security umbrella still functions.

Third, escalation now can prevent a larger war later because a ceasefire that is already being violated is not stable. This matters because if Iran learns that it can probe US resolve without major consequences, it will keep testing red lines until a much bigger crisis forces a worse and less controlled response.

opp_args.thesis: The US should avoid military escalation and prioritize a negotiated settlement because force in the Strait of Hormuz is more likely to produce regional war than compliance.
mechanisms: First, military pressure can backfire by hardening Iranian resolve. One, it strengthens Iranian hardliners who argue the US cannot be trusted; two, it makes compromise look like surrender domestically; three, it reduces the space for moderates or mediators like Pakistan to sell a deal.

Second, escalation risks immediate economic and security spillovers. One, the Strait of Hormuz is a global energy chokepoint, so even short disruptions can spike oil prices and hurt allies; two, attacks on UAE territory show the conflict can widen beyond the bilateral US-Iran track; three, once ships and coastal sites are hit, miscalculation becomes much more likely than controlled signaling.

Third, diplomacy is the only route to a durable outcome because the core dispute is the nuclear file, not just the naval clash. One, airstrikes cannot verify or cap Iran’s nuclear program; two, a memorandum of understanding can create sequencing and monitoring; three, a ceasefire that survives only through threats is inherently unstable.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether coercion produces compliance or collapse. Pro wins if you believe Iran is strategically vulnerable and deterrable; Opp wins if you think the Strait of Hormuz makes any show of force too economically and militarily contagious to control.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would maintain military pressure on Iran despite a fragile ceasefire
THBT the US should prioritize coercive deterrence over immediate diplomacy in the Strait of Hormuz crisis
THP a world where great powers respond to ceasefire violations with immediate limited force

cards.title: Australia’s IS Returnees Force a Clash Between Repatriation, Justice, and Counterterrorism
cards.background: Three Australian women with links to the Islamic State were formally charged after returning from Syria. Kawsar Ahmad, 53, and her daughter Zeinab Ahmad, 31, were arrested at Melbourne airport and charged with crimes against humanity; police allege Kawsar was complicit in the purchase of a female slave for US$10,000 and both women knowingly kept a slave in their home. In Sydney, Janai Safar, 32, was charged with entering and remaining in a declared conflict zone and joining IS. The three are part of a larger cohort of 34 Australian women and children who had been living at the al-Roj camp in Syria since 2019, and the Australian government had previously refused to assist their return.

prop_args.thesis: Australia should aggressively prosecute returning IS-linked nationals to signal that citizenship does not shield atrocity crimes and to deter future foreign-fighter participation.
mechanisms: First, prosecution restores deterrence and raises the expected cost of joining extremist groups. This is because (1) foreign-fighter travel often relies on the assumption that women and family members will be treated leniently, (2) visible arrests at the airport show that return does not equal impunity, and (3) long prison terms — up to 25 years for crimes against humanity — create a credible threat that can shape future decisions by would-be recruits and facilitators.

Second, it protects domestic security by incapacitating people who may still hold extremist networks, ideology, or facilitation capacity. Three reasons: one, returnees can act as nodes for radicalization inside diaspora communities; two, some may have logistical knowledge about recruitment, financing, and travel routes; three, the state reduces monitoring burdens by moving the highest-risk cases into custody and the criminal justice system.

Third, prosecution is necessary for justice and legitimacy because the alleged conduct involves slavery and membership in a genocidal organization. This matters because (1) victims of IS crimes need recognition that their abuse is treated as serious international criminal conduct, (2) failure to prosecute would create a perception of double standards between domestic offenders and overseas atrocity perpetrators, and (3) a court process creates evidentiary records that can support broader accountability for IS crimes.

opp_args.thesis: Australia should prioritize repatriation, rehabilitation, and child protection over high-profile prosecutions that may be symbolically satisfying but strategically counterproductive.
mechanisms: First, criminal prosecution can be a blunt tool that does little to reduce long-term extremism. One, many returnees are family members rather than frontline combatants, so blanket punishment risks overestimating individual culpability; two, prison can harden identities and reinforce extremist narratives of persecution; three, incarceration without deradicalization may simply delay the security problem rather than solve it.

Second, the state has a duty to manage the children and family members in these cohorts humanely and pragmatically. One, children cannot be treated as responsible for parental affiliations and need education, healthcare, and social reintegration; two, keeping families in limbo in camps like al-Roj creates a humanitarian and security vacuum where radicalization is more likely; three, controlled repatriation allows authorities to monitor, support, and separate risk profiles more effectively than abandonment abroad.

Third, overreliance on prosecutions can weaken rule-of-law credibility if evidence is thin or politically charged. One, crimes committed in Syria are hard to prove to domestic criminal standards years later; two, selective enforcement can look like punishment driven by public outrage rather than individualized guilt; three, if cases collapse or appear unfair, the government loses legitimacy and strengthens extremist propaganda about Western injustice.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between short-term punitive signaling and long-term security management. Prosecution wins if you think deterrence and accountability are the priority; repatriation wins if you think the real problem is preventing future radicalization and managing children and low-risk family members in a controlled environment.
motion_areas: TH, as Australia, would prosecute all returning IS-linked nationals to the fullest extent of the law
THBT states should repatriate citizens from foreign ISIS camps and process them domestically
THP a world where women and family members of foreign fighters are treated as full security risks rather than presumed dependents

cards.title: Trump-Lula Rapprochement Masks Deep US-Brazil Frictions Over Trade, Crime, and Bolsonaro
cards.background: US President Donald Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva met privately at the White House for around three hours on Thursday. Trump later called the meeting "very good" and Lula said he left "very satisfied," but there was no joint Oval Office press appearance, which observers read as a sign that major disputes remain unresolved. The two governments still disagree over trade tariffs, organised crime, the US war in Iran, possible American interference in Brazil's October elections, and Trump's push for Lula to drop charges against former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted last year of an attempted coup and sentenced to 27 years in prison.

prop_args.thesis: A quiet, pragmatic reset between Trump and Lula is the best outcome for both countries because it reduces escalation risk without requiring immediate agreement on every dispute.
mechanisms: First, de-escalation lowers the probability of a self-reinforcing diplomatic spiral. This is because (1) public humiliation or press theatrics would harden domestic audiences on both sides, (2) once leaders are boxed into nationalist postures they have fewer off-ramps on tariffs, crime cooperation, and election interference, and (3) a private channel preserves bargaining space for later concessions.

Second, the meeting creates a working relationship that is especially valuable under Trump-style personal diplomacy. Three reasons: one, Trump responds more to personal rapport than to institutional process, two, a three-hour private meeting signals direct leader-to-leader access that can bypass bureaucratic deadlock, and three, it allows Lula to manage friction without publicly conceding on Bolsonaro or sovereignty.

Third, avoiding public conflict is itself a strategic win for Brazil in an asymmetric relationship. This matters because (1) the US is more important to Brazil than vice versa, (2) Brazil can preserve trade and security channels while waiting for a more favorable negotiating window, and (3) with elections looming in both countries, neither side wants to hand opponents a visible diplomatic crisis.

opp_args.thesis: The meeting is mostly cosmetic because the core disputes are structural and will keep generating conflict regardless of cordial optics.
mechanisms: First, the underlying policy disagreements are too deep to be solved by personal diplomacy. One, the sides remain far apart on trade and tariffs, two, the US and Brazil disagree on crime and on whether Brazil should classify certain groups as terrorist organisations, and three, Trump is still pressuring Lula on Bolsonaro, which directly collides with Brazilian judicial sovereignty.

Second, the absence of a joint press appearance suggests both leaders know there is no substantive breakthrough. One, if the meeting had produced real concessions, both sides would have wanted to showcase them publicly, two, the lack of a joint statement implies unresolved bargaining, and three, the private format may simply be damage control to avoid exposing failure.

Third, the asymmetry of power means Brazil may be forced into concessions later even if the meeting looked friendly. One, the US can use tariffs, diplomatic pressure, and security leverage, two, Brazil has fewer tools to retaliate without harming its own economy, and three, election timing may delay rather than resolve the dispute, making the current calm temporary.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether diplomacy is judged by immediate policy wins or by preventing escalation. Prop wins if the round is about crisis management and preserving bargaining space; opp wins if the round is about whether the meeting actually changed the underlying balance of power, because the structural disputes over trade, sovereignty, and Bolsonaro remain intact.
motion_areas: TH, as Brazil, would prioritize quiet diplomacy with the United States over public confrontation
THBT middle powers should avoid public escalation with more powerful states even when core disputes remain unresolved
THP a world where leaders resolve bilateral disputes through private meetings rather than public summits

cards.title: US Passport Revocations Turn Child Support Debt Into a Mobility Sanction
cards.background: The US State Department said it will begin revoking passports of Americans who owe more than $2,500 in child support debt, using a rarely enforced 1996 federal law. Previously, passport penalties were mainly applied when delinquent parents tried to renew their passports; under the new policy, the government will work with the Department of Health and Human Services to identify debtors and revoke passports proactively. Those whose passports are revoked cannot use them for travel and will not be eligible for a new passport until the debt is paid, though people abroad may seek an emergency travel document from a US embassy or consulate to return home.

prop_args.thesis: Revoking passports is an effective coercive tool that increases child support compliance and improves welfare for children who are owed money.
mechanisms: First, it raises the cost of non-payment by targeting a valuable privilege that many debtors cannot easily substitute. This works because (1) international mobility is important for work, family, and emergencies, (2) losing a passport creates immediate personal inconvenience beyond a distant court order, and (3) the threat is credible because the State Department can enforce it directly through existing federal law.

Second, it improves collection rates by converting a civil debt into a high-salience enforcement mechanism. Three reasons: one, many delinquent parents ignore ordinary arrears notices because the consequences are abstract; two, passport revocation creates a concrete deadline to pay or negotiate; three, the policy can be administered at scale through data-sharing between federal agencies and state child support offices.

Third, it protects children and custodial parents by prioritizing repayment over debtor convenience. This matters because (1) child support is often used for essentials like housing, food, and school costs, (2) unpaid support disproportionately harms lower-income single-parent households, and (3) the state has a stronger justification to use hard enforcement here than in ordinary consumer debt because the obligation is tied to child welfare.

opp_args.thesis: Passport revocation is a blunt punishment that is likely to be counterproductive, especially for low-income parents, and may reduce rather than increase child support payments.
mechanisms: First, it can destroy the debtor's ability to earn and therefore pay. One, many parents need travel for work, especially in jobs involving sales, construction, logistics, or cross-border family obligations; two, taking away mobility can reduce employment opportunities and income; three, lower income means less ability to clear arrears, creating a vicious cycle.

Second, it is an inequitable enforcement tool that punishes inability to pay as if it were refusal to pay. One, the $2,500 threshold can capture parents with unstable employment or medical shocks rather than deliberate evaders; two, revocation hits hardest on people who already lack legal and financial resources; three, it turns a child-support system into a regressive sanction that may deepen poverty in the very households it is meant to help.

Third, it creates administrative and humanitarian risks without solving the underlying enforcement problem. One, people abroad may be stranded or forced into emergency consular processes; two, federal-state data matching can produce errors, delays, and due-process disputes; three, aggressive punishment may push parents further underground, making future collection and co-parenting cooperation harder.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the policy changes behavior more than it worsens debtors' ability to pay. Prop wins if the sanction is seen as a targeted, credible nudge against deliberate non-payment; opp wins if the key population is actually cash-strapped parents for whom mobility is economically productive and revocation is self-defeating.
stock_connections: Ability to Pay vs Willingness to Pay

THBT states should use mobility restrictions to enforce family court judgments
